sentences.text: Coelophysis is considered one of the earliest known dinosaur genera, a lightly built animal that measured up to 3 meters in length and stood more than one meter tall at the hips.
The generic name Coelophysis refers to the hollow bones found in its legs, and the animal possessed an elongated snout with large openings that helped reduce skull weight.
The Ghost Ranch excavation yielded hundreds of Coelophysis skeletons in a single concentration, described as the greatest Triassic find in North America.
Evidence of cannibalism was found in specimen NMMNH P-44551, which contained regurgitated material including fragments of juvenile Coelophysis teeth and jaw bones.
Coelophysis was the second dinosaur to travel to space, with a skull from the Carnegie Museum of Natural History aboard the Space Shuttle Endeavour mission STS-89 on January 22, 1998.
It was designated the official state fossil of New Mexico, with C. bauri specifically becoming the state fossil in 1981.
It is one of the oldest dinosaurs for which the presence of feathers has been suggested.
The type species Coelophysis bauri was described by Edward Drinker Cope in 1889, originally having been placed in the genus Coelurus in 1887.
Excavations at the Ghost Ranch Coelophysis quarry continued through 1947 and 1948 by the American Museum of Natural History crew.
Coelophysis possessed blade-like, recurved, sharp, and finely serrated teeth on both edges, typical of predatory dinosaurs, with approximately 26 teeth in its upper jaw and 27 teeth in the lower jaw.
Evidence suggests it ate meat, likely small animals such as lizards found near its fossils.
Variation in proportions among individuals of the same size suggests the existence of 'robust' and 'gracile' morphs within Coelophysis.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the weight of Coelophysis at 15 kg for the gracile form, 20 kg for the robust form, and later revised the estimate to 25 kg.
Coelophysis likely reached sexual maturity between its second and third year of life and attained a full length of just over 10 feet by its eighth year.
The average Coelophysis egg was estimated to be 31–33.5 mm across its minor diameter, with females laying 24 to 26 eggs per clutch.
The tail's lattice structure may have helped the animal maneuver at high speeds.
Researchers suggest the large congregation of Coelophysis at Ghost Ranch may have gathered to feed or drink before being buried by a flash flood or drought.
The discovery of 30 specimens of C. rhodesiensis found together in Zimbabwe has led some paleontologists to suggest Coelophysis was gregarious.
Research indicates that Coelophysis lived in floodplain environments with distinct dry and wet seasons.
Research in 2026 reconstructed the optimal jumping performance of C. bauri as similar to that of the elegant crested tinamou.
All material from the Ghost Ranch quarry was classified as a single species of Coelophysis known from hundreds of individuals.
Coelophysis was designated a nomen conservandum, resolving the taxonomic confusion regarding its status.
Independent work by Sterling Nesbitt, Randall Irmis, and William Parker in 2007 upheld the identification of Eucoelophysis as a silesaurid, distant from Coelophysis and the Baldwin material.
Coelophysis fossils from Ghost Ranch were found in the Chinle Formation, which was believed to be of Norian age at the time of discovery.
Hunt and Lucas argued that Coelophysis lived in the Revueltian-age Petrified Forest Formation, while Rioarribasaurus lived in the older Apachean-age Rock Point Formation.
C. rhodesiensis fossils have been recovered from the Upper Elliot Formation in South Africa and the Forest Sandstone Formation in Zimbabwe.
It is debated whether Megapnosaurus was once a species within Coelophysis, but it is now considered a valid genus.
Some researchers debate the validity of Coelophysis as a distinct genus, suggesting it is a 'metataxon' lacking unique characteristics.
